newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans flee rebel-targeted Kisangani by river.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans flee rebel-targeted Kisangani by river.

text.p: Hordes of civilians have taken to dugout canoes plying the vast Zaire river at night to escape an expected rebel attack on the eastern Zairean city of Kisangani, travellers said on Sunday.
Several sources in Kisangani said by telephone the jungle city was heavily mined by government troops and their largely Serb mercenary backers to check the rebel advance.

The minefield could be a deadly trap not only for invading rebels but hundreds of thousands of unsuspecting Hutu refugees trudging through the jungle to reach Kisangani after being displaced by fighting from nearby towns and villages.
Also at risk are impoverished civilian city folk with no means to escape by air as wealthier residents have been doing.

"Lots of people are leaving Kisangani by the river at night. I spent last night on the river and saw many pirogues coming downstream," said a missionary who reached Kisangani airport after travelling 100 km (60 miles) up river in a canoe.
Some reports said soldiers had set up check-points downstream from Kisangani and were stopping passing boats.
The 150 or so people lucky enough to get on a flight out on Saturday talked of fighting north of Kisangani although they reported that the city itself was calm but tense.

Aid agency officials flew deep into rebel-held territory on Sunday, trying to spot the Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees. They include former Rwandan troops and militiamen who fled Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
They say they will be killed by the Tutsi-led rebels.
The rebels accepted a U.N. call for talks with the beleaguered government of President Mobutu Sese Seko but rejected a truce.

Mobutu, who set himself up as the only man who could hold the nation of over 200 different ethnic groups together, had cancer surgery in Europe last August. He has spent little time in Zaire since then and is now at his villa on the French Riviera.

The rebels have been fighting since October to end 31 years of rule by Mobutu, accused by opponents of colossal corruption and mismanagement that has impoverished a country with one of the world's largest mineral reserves.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said the southern and central mining regions of Shaba and Kasai were priorities for his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL), which has already seized about a sixth of Zaire.

"Things are going very well on the military front. We are already halfway into Shaba and in the next week we will be headed further towards Kasai," he told journalists at his base in the eastern border town of Goma on Saturday.
Kabila said Kisangani would fall despite stiff resistance from ethnic Hutu soldiers of the former Rwandan army.
At the same time he said he could accept a five-point U.N. plan as a basis for negotiations, but he rejected the first, and most important -- a ceasefire before talks.
At the head of the navigable part of the Zaire River, Kisangani is also potentially the most significant rebel target since they took up arms from the eastern border with Rwanda.
Airport and defence ministry sources and civilians arriving in Kinshasa said there had been no notable reports of fighting near the city over the previous two days.
Zaire turned to mercenaries after accusing Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending their army troops to back the Tutsi-led rebels. All three neighbours deny the charge.
Zaire's notoriously indisciplined army has been unable to stop the highly motivated rebels. The army's penchant for looting has driven disgusted civilians into the rebel fold.
